prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The produce bins occupy the lower foreground, roughly 0.3–1 m from the camera, while the wall and store interior lie several metres behind them; brighter fruit and bin edges help separate these depth layers. Across frames 1–3, the camera shifts laterally past adjacent bins, with overlapping rims showing which containers are in front of others; in frames 4–5, a person is approximately 0.7–1.5 m ahead and moves closer or becomes more fully framed. The person faces generally toward the camera wearer, but gaze direction is not reliably encoded by depth, and the head and torso are partly cropped by the frame boundaries. The map makes relative distance and occlusion boundaries clearer than RGB, but its saturated bright wall regions, flattened person silhouettes, and inconsistent brightness on similarly placed produce make metre estimates unreliable.
descriptions.segmentation: The map locates several apple groups across the left and central produce display, one orange region near the lower centre, and people in the two rightmost frames; the masks clarify which visible regions belong to separate object instances despite overlap. The produce is in front of the background and mostly within about 0.3–1 m of the camera wearer, while the large person masks are roughly 0.7–1.5 m ahead; exact distances and distances between instances cannot be recovered from segmentation alone. In frames 4–5 the main person is near the centre-right and then far right, facing roughly toward the camera wearer, while a much smaller person region in frame 5 is farther away and left of the nearer person. The map is unreliable where it omits baskets, yellow produce, and much of the surrounding scene, fragments or overlaps apple masks and labels, and crops masks at image boundaries; it also provides no direct facing, gaze, reach, or depth measurement.
descriptions.pose: The pose map detects only a small cluster of yellow facial or upper-body keypoints on the person in frames 4 and 5, placing that person ahead and first near centre-right, then near the far-right edge. The keypoint arrangement is consistent with the person facing broadly toward the camera wearer, but it is too sparse to determine precise gaze, body orientation, limb position, or whether either person can reach nearby objects. No usable skeleton appears for frames 1–3, and no magenta hand keypoints are visible, so the map adds no spatial information about the produce, arm’s reach, or object occlusion there. Relative to RGB, it makes the detected person’s changing image position easier to track, but missing torso and limb joints, boundary cropping, and the absence of a skeleton for the smaller background person make it highly incomplete and unsuitable for estimating metric distance.
